summary: Defines the offer/answer model, in which one party describes a desired multimedia session using SDP and the other replies with its own description to agree on a shared view. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3264 defines how two endpoints negotiate a multimedia call. One proposes what they want to use, the other responds with what they can accept, so both agree on a common set of media streams.

what is the sdp offer answer model
how to put a call on hold with sdp
subtitle: How two endpoints trade SDP descriptions to agree on a shared view of a unicast session.

tldr.problem: SDP describes sessions, but for a unicast session the two participants must agree on parameters such as addresses and a common set of codecs.
tldr.mechanism: One side sends an offer listing streams, codecs, addresses and ports. The other replies with an answer that matches each stream in order, accepting or rejecting each one.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3264 is the mandatory baseline for SIP and has been updated by RFC 6157, RFC 8843 and RFC 9143. It obsoletes RFC 2543.

facts.label: RTCP port
facts.value: One higher than RTP port by default

today: RFC 3264 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2543 and has been updated by RFC 6157, RFC 8843 and RFC 9143.

sections.title: Why a Model Is Needed
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) was originally designed for multicast sessions where all participants share one view. For unicast sessions, two participants need to agree on parameters: each needs its own address and port information, and they must find a common set of codecs.

RFC 3264 defines the offer/answer model to solve this. An offer lists what one side wants and can provide; an answer lists what the other side accepts. The model is independent of how SDP is carried; it is the mandatory baseline for SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: For a call between two people, each person must say where to reach them and what they can do. The offer/answer model lets them trade this information until they agree.

sections.title: Basic Rules and Glare
sections.content:
The higher-layer protocol carries SDP and keeps context. The offerer sends an offer; the answerer may answer or reject it. The exchange is atomic: if the answer is rejected, the session returns to the state before the offer.

Either side may send a new offer at any time to update the session, but not while it holds an unanswered offer from the peer or while its own offer is still waiting for an answer. If an offer arrives after sending one but before receiving an answer, this is glare; because offers may not be sent while waiting for an answer, the higher-layer protocol (such as SIP) must resolve glare according to its own rules.
sections.plainLanguage: One person proposes, the other responds. They take turns and do not make new proposals while waiting for a reply.

sections.title: Generating the Initial Offer
sections.content:
An offer must be a valid SDP message (it may omit e and p lines) and must contain exactly one session description. For unicast, the s= line should be a single space or dash, and for streams created/destroyed by outside signaling, t= should be 0 0.

Each media stream has a direction (sendrecv default, sendonly, recvonly, inactive). For streams the offerer wants to receive, the m= line gives the port and transport; RTCP goes to the port one higher by default. A port of zero means the stream is not wanted.

Formats on the m= line must be in preference order (first is most preferred). For RTP streams, a=rtpmap lines map payload types to encodings. Multiple streams of the same or different media types may be offered.
sections.plainLanguage: The offer lists each media stream with its mailbox (port), what kinds of formats it supports (in order of preference), and whether it wants to send, receive, both, or neither.

sections.title: Generating the Answer
sections.content:
The answer must have the same number of m= lines as the offer, in the same order. The t= line must equal the offer's. If the answer differs from the offer in any way, its origin line must be different, because a different entity wrote it.

To reject a stream, set its port to zero. If no media format is shared, the answerer must reject that stream; if no format is shared for any stream, the whole session is rejected. Directions must be compatible (e.g. sendonly in offer pairs with recvonly in answer; inactive pairs with inactive).

The answer lists formats it can use in its own preference order (though it is recommended to keep the offer's relative order). The offerer must send using a format from the answer and should use the first one listed. For multicast, constraints are stricter.

For each accepted stream the answerer may list one or more formats it can use; the set of formats in the answer is the intersection of the offered set and what the answerer accepts, written in the answerer's order of preference (though preserving the offer's relative order is recommended). Once negotiated, media proceeds using those parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The responder matches each proposed stream one by one. For each, they either reject it (port zero) or accept it and say which of the proposed formats they prefer and in which direction they will send/receive.

sections.title: Updating a Session
sections.content:
Session changes use the same offer/answer procedure. The new offer repeats the previous SDP with the version number in the o= line incremented by one. The number of m= lines must not decrease (deleted streams keep a slot with port zero; new streams can reuse such slots).

When changing ports, addresses, or transport, the sender must be ready to receive on both old and new until media arrives on the new one. The mapping from a dynamic payload type to a codec must not change for the duration of the session. A format is considered gone if ports change, dynamic payload types change, or after a short timer (one minute is typically sufficient).

To put a stream on hold, mark sendrecv as sendonly or recvonly as inactive (the old practice of using connection address 0.0.0.0 is discouraged). An SDP reporting capabilities may use port zero on all media lines so it cannot be misread as starting a stream.
sections.plainLanguage: To change something, propose a new description with a bumped version number. Keep both ends ready for old and new addresses briefly during the switch, and never shrink the list of streams without leaving empty slots.

sections.title: Indicating Capabilities
sections.content: An SDP description may list capabilities instead of starting a session. To avoid being misread as an offer, such a description sets the port to zero on all m= lines. The offer/answer rules above still apply when this capability description is used in an exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: A description can list what an endpoint is able to do without beginning a session, so that callers know what to ask for.
